Countries trade because they have different resources. A country can often produce a good more cheaply than other nations when it has easy access to the raw materials, up to date technology, or specially skilled workers that the product requires. Nations are most efficient when they produce the products their resources are best suited for and trade for the rest. Import limits, freedom from tariffs, or a high standard of living do not by themselves make production cheaper. Example: a country with large iron ore deposits can make steel at lower cost than a country that must import the ore.

term: Business Ethics and Impact on Others
definition: A business's ethics are its standards for deciding whether an action is acceptable, and those standards matter most when an action could have a negative impact on others: employees, customers, suppliers, or the community. Anything illegal is unacceptable no matter what the business's ethics say, and profit or environmental impact are only two of many factors weighed. Example: a company decides not to cut a safety step that would save money because the change could harm customers.

term: Government Stimulating the Flow of Money
definition: The federal government can speed up or slow down the flow of money in the economy. To stimulate the flow of money, it increases government services and spending or lowers taxes, which puts more money into circulation. To restrict the flow of money, it raises taxes, spends less (buys fewer goods and services), or raises interest rates on borrowing. Example: funding new highway projects and expanding public services pumps money into the economy.

Productivity cannot be improved until it has been measured. Businesses measure the efficiency of their current production methods to find out whether improvements are needed and how to make them. Measuring productivity is not done to decide whether salaries should change. Example: a factory times how long each unit takes to assemble, discovers a slow station, and reorganizes the work area to speed it up.

term: Profit as the Ultimate Goal of New Markets
definition: When a company redirects its marketing effort toward an untapped market segment, its ultimate goal is to increase profit. Creating demand among new customers raises sales, and higher sales raise profits. Increasing output may be necessary to serve the new market, but that is a means, not the end goal; raising expenses lowers profit, and raising prices could reduce sales. Example: a snack company that starts marketing to college students hopes the added sales will boost its bottom line.

Small businesses benefit their local communities in several ways. They pay taxes that fund government services community members use, such as roads, schools, and trash removal. They also provide jobs and increase competition, which gives consumers more choices. Charging interest is not a community benefit because it helps the business rather than the community. Example: property and sales taxes paid by a local bakery help pay for the town's public services.

term: Union Organization Levels: Local, National, Federation
definition: Unions are organized in levels. A local union is the lowest level and represents workers at a specific company or in a specific geographic area. A national (or international) union is made up of many local unions and helps establish new locals. A federation is the highest level: a group of several different national unions that join together for common purposes such as public relations and political goals. Example: the AFL CIO is a federation made up of many national unions.

A franchise lets a person open a business using an established company's name and system. The biggest advantage is a well known brand name, which brings an existing customer base and raises the chance of success compared with an unknown new business; other advantages are training and ongoing support. Disadvantages include paying an initial fee and ongoing royalties and accepting restrictions on products, prices, and location. Reliance on raw materials is a drawback of manufacturing, not of franchising.

Possession utility is the usefulness created when ownership of a product is transferred from the seller to the buyer. Marketers add possession utility mainly through personal selling, since salespeople help customers choose the right goods and services and complete the purchase. Compare: delivery and distribution create place utility (product is where the customer wants it), and developing new products creates form utility (product is in a useful form). Example: a salesperson who helps a customer pick and buy the right laptop adds possession utility.

Utility is the usefulness or value a product provides. Form utility comes from changing the shape or form of materials into a more useful product. Time utility comes from making products available when customers want them. Place utility comes from making products available where customers want them. Possession utility comes from transferring ownership from seller to buyer. Example: a campus bookstore stocking required textbooks creates place utility because students need the books right there on campus.

Compliance technology is software that helps a business follow laws and regulations. Its positive impacts include identifying patterns and trends in company data (which leads to better risk assessment), improving overall efficiency, and protecting private data so a breach is less likely. It does not replace human compliance specialists: a computer can analyze information and draw conclusions, but a person must decide what to do with them.

term: Regulations as a Source of Economic Risk
definition: Government laws and regulations are designed to protect consumers, workers, and the environment, but they can also create economic risk for businesses because they can reduce profits. Rules that require paying for environmental cleanups, buying special licenses, or recalling a product can cost a company a great deal of money. Example: a new regulation requiring expensive pollution controls lowers a factory's profits even though it makes the community safer.

Shareholders, including companies that own stock in other companies, must pay income taxes on the dividends they receive. Capital gains taxes apply only when an investor sells securities for more than they paid, not when dividends are earned. Sales taxes apply to purchased items, and excise taxes are charged on specific goods such as gasoline and alcohol. Example: a company that receives quarterly dividends on 100 shares of another company's stock owes income tax on those dividends.

Internal records such as inventory lists, sales records, and expense reports are a valuable source of business information, and owners should monitor them regularly. Reviewing inventory records shows which products sell well and which do not, so the business can order the right amount of each item and avoid overstocking or running out. Example: a hardware store owner checks her inventory list every month and adjusts her orders based on which products moved.

term: Online Information Storage: Benefits and Downsides
definition: Storing information online (in the cloud or on company servers) is usually cheaper than paper storage, makes information easier to access, and lets data be sorted and searched quickly. The main downside is that it is so easy to keep everything that a business can end up with far too much data, leading to information overload and even system overload. Businesses should decide what is worth keeping instead of saving every file. Example: a company that never deletes old email attachments finds its shared drive so cluttered that employees cannot find current files.

Quality records are records that are accurate and reliable, so an employee who uses them gets correct results. Whether a record is on paper or digital, or whether the law requires it to be kept, does not make it a quality record. Businesses check and update records so that phone numbers, addresses, and other details stay correct. Example: an employee calls a client using the number on file and reaches the wrong person, showing that the record was not a quality record.

Statistics are information presented in numerical form, and businesses analyze them to spot trends, measure profitability, and evaluate performance, including the success of promotions. When interpreting statistics, draw only the conclusions the numbers actually support. Example: if sales rose 28 percent during the two weeks a TV commercial ran, the business can conclude the promotion boosted short term sales, but it cannot conclude which items sold best, whether it should have ordered more inventory, or that sales will keep rising.

The purpose of data mining is to turn raw data into useful information. It involves examining large quantities of data and extracting the patterns and insights that help a company understand its customers better, increase sales, and reduce costs. Data mining is not done to sell consumer information, monitor competitors, or keep employees engaged. Example: a grocery chain mines years of checkout data and discovers which products are usually bought together, then places them near each other.

Information technology (IT) refers to the technical parts of handling information: hardware, software, and networks. An information system (IS) is broader: it manages an entire set of information and includes the technology plus the people and the processes that use it. In other words, information systems put extra emphasis on the people involved. Example: a hospital's servers and software are its IT, while the nurses, doctors, and procedures that use patient records together with that technology make up its information system.

Slides made with presentation software are visual aids that support an oral presentation, so each slide should contain key points that highlight or reinforce the most important information. Numerical data belongs only where it supports a point. Colorful graphics and creative transitions can add interest but are not required on every slide, and too many can distract from the message.

Presentation software (such as PowerPoint or Google Slides) lets a user build slide shows that combine text, graphics, photographs, animation, and sound into one lively visual presentation. Its purpose is to present information to an audience in an appealing way. It is not designed to connect computers on a network, copy and print documents, or calculate mathematical data (spreadsheet software does the math).

Project management software comes with different capabilities. Cost assignment and tracking functions store and calculate accounting information such as expenses and amortization, which is useful for large projects with hundreds of activities. Resource scheduling and leveling functions schedule materials, equipment, and people and help balance workloads and bottlenecks. Task delegation and charting functions (such as Gantt charts) document who is doing what and when. Example: a construction firm uses the cost tracking function to compare budgeted and actual spending on each phase.

Satellite technology uses satellites orbiting the earth to send and receive signals, and it powers the global positioning system (GPS) that map apps on smartphones use to find your location and give directions. It is different from an expert system (software that imitates a human expert's knowledge), hardware (the physical parts of a computer), and telecommuting (working from a remote location). Example: a salesperson enters a client's address in a map app before a long drive, and the app uses satellite signals to guide her turn by turn.

term: Search Engine Keywords and Query Field
definition: To find business information with a search engine, type specific keywords (terms or phrases that describe your topic) into the query field, the box where the search is entered, and click search. The more specific the keywords, the more useful the results. Vague or general terms return too many unrelated results. Example: typing 'Washington' returns pages about the state, the capital, and the president, but 'Washington state manufacturers' returns the manufacturers you wanted.

Spreadsheet software (such as Excel or Google Sheets) lets users enter numbers in rows and columns and then performs calculations and analysis automatically. Its standard function is performing accounting, financial, and other mathematical work, such as building budgets, projecting sales, or totaling expenses. Other tasks belong to other software types: presentation software creates slide shows, desktop publishing software creates brochures, and database software manages database files. Example: a manager uses a spreadsheet to calculate next quarter's budget projections.

After a webpage is designed, it must be posted on a web host (a web server run by a hosting company or internet service provider) so people can reach it online; hosts may charge a fee to post and store the pages. The business also registers its domain name, the web address users type to reach the site, either directly through ICANN or through the web host. A hyperlink, modem, or Ethernet connection does not need to be registered. Example: a new bakery picks a hosting company and registers sweetcrumbs.com.

Many businesses include an email inquiry field or contact form on their website so customers can send questions, report problems, or give feedback. This is an effective customer service tool as long as the business responds promptly. Other website features serve different purposes: a Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) page provides answers rather than collecting feedback, and a product catalog displays merchandise. Example: a customer uses the 'Contact Us' form to report that a product arrived damaged, and the company replies within a day.

Online product reviews are opinions and experiences that other buyers post on consumer information websites, blogs, and retailer sites. Shoppers read them before buying so they can make an informed buying decision based on how real users rate a product. Reviews are different from price comparison tools or reaffirming a purchase already made. Example: a student reads dozens of phone reviews on a popular website to decide which model to buy, then visits stores to compare prices.

When evaluating an online source, presentation is the criterion that looks at how the information is communicated: clarity of language, readable font size, clean layout, effective colors, useful graphics, and clear audio or video. Presentation matters because so much reading is done on screens. It is separate from relevance (does the information fit the topic), objectivity (is it unbiased), and timeliness (is it up to date). Example: a well organized page with readable text scores high on presentation even if its data is old.

Promotional records are documents that hold information about the communications a business uses to inform, persuade, or remind customers about its products, image, or ideas. Businesses keep them for two key reasons: to time future promotions appropriately and to evaluate how effective past promotions were. They are different from inventory records (stock levels), personnel records (employee promotions and reviews), and payroll records (wages and overtime). Example: a record showing that a spring coupon campaign boosted sales tells the business when to run it again.

Financial records contain private information, so a business shares them only when there is a good reason. The most common reason is to prove the business's net worth and financial health to a bank when applying for a loan. Financial records would not be shown to competitors or suppliers, and they say little about the quality of a business's service. Example: a small business submits its balance sheet and income statement to a bank so the lender can see what the business owns and owes.

term: Table of Contents in Business Reports
definition: A table of contents lists the sections of a business report with their page numbers so readers can navigate a long document and find specific information quickly. Title pages, introductions, and appendices are also useful, but their main purpose is not to help readers locate information: the title page identifies the report, the introduction explains its purpose, and the appendix holds supporting material. Example: a 40 page market report with a table of contents lets a manager jump straight to the pricing section.

The ending of a web address gives a clue about how trustworthy its information is. A site ending in .gov can only be owned and operated by a government body, so its information is more likely to be researched and reliable. A site ending in .com can be owned by anyone, so its content must be checked more carefully. The domain ending says nothing about how recent the information is. Example: for statistics on unemployment, a .gov labor department page is generally more trustworthy than a random .com blog.

Controlling expenses is one way a business increases profits, and floor or display space is an expense because the business pays for every square foot. Using display space effectively, by keeping it organized, attractive, and stocked with items customers want, raises sales per square foot and may let the business use less space overall. Expanding promotion, borrowing more, or shifting funds around does not control expenses. Example: a store that consolidates scattered displays into one appealing area saves on space costs and sells more at the same time.

Businesses change their processes for different reasons: to improve productivity (getting work done faster with the same resources), to improve quality, to manage risk, or to improve the customer experience. To identify the driver, look at what problem the change solves. If the concern is the time employees spend on tasks, the driver is productivity. Example: a call center that has agents specialize in specific procedures so requests are handled faster is making a productivity driven process change.

Managing a global supply chain brings special challenges: accountability and compliance, language barriers, time zone differences, and delivery and shipping delays. Accountability and compliance means a company is held responsible for its overseas partners following safety regulations, child labor laws, and fair pay practices, and it can face public backlash and lost sales if a foreign factory breaks those rules. Companies should review these issues before joining a global supply chain. Example: a clothing brand loses customers after a supplier's factory is found violating workplace safety laws.

Every business takes inputs and turns them into outputs. Inputs are the resources a business uses, such as employees, raw materials, equipment, and capital. Outputs are what the business produces, meaning its goods and services, which together are called products. Example: for a bakery, the bakers, flour, and ovens are inputs, while the bread and cakes are outputs.

Logistics is the operations activity that manages the flow of goods and services from production to consumption. It includes all the people, information, and processes involved in storing and transporting goods, so decisions about how to ship products are logistics decisions. It is different from scheduling (setting the production timetable), safety and security (protecting people from hazards), and maintenance and repairs (keeping equipment working). Example: choosing whether to move goods by truck or by rail is a logistics decision.

term: Monitoring Accounts Receivable in the Budget
definition: A budget lists projected figures next to actual results, and a business monitors it to spot problems and make adjustments. If the budget shows that a large amount of accounts receivable is past due, the business has a collection problem and must act quickly, because old accounts are hard to collect and can turn into bad debts. Credit card and personal check sales bring in cash quickly and do not create bad debt, and high cash receipts are a good sign, not a warning. Example: a supplier that notices many customer invoices are 90 days overdue should step up collection efforts before the money is lost.

Payroll is one of a business's largest expenses, and it is the expense employees can most directly help control. When employees arrive on time and work their full scheduled hours, the business gets full value for every payroll dollar. Other big expenses such as rent, taxes, and advertising are set by contracts, governments, or management and are outside an individual employee's control. Example: a cashier who shows up on time every shift helps the store avoid paying for time that was not worked.

term: Process Design Requirements: Goal, Single Owner, Limited Scope
definition: When a business uses process thinking to design a process, every process must have a goal, and its outputs are measured against that goal; each process should also support the organization's overall goals. A process should have a single owner who is responsible for its output, and a clearly defined, limited scope. A process does not have a deadline of its own, because it is the repeatable method used to meet goals and deadlines. Example: an order fulfillment process has the goal of shipping every order within 24 hours and one manager who owns it.

Production is the activity of creating the goods and services consumers want. It is called a conversion process because it takes a business's resources (inputs such as materials, labor, and equipment) and converts them into salable products (outputs). Product utility, meaning the usefulness of a product, is a result of production, not the reason for the name. Example: a furniture maker converts lumber, fabric, and labor into finished chairs.

Companies change their business processes for reasons such as improving performance, reducing costs, and increasing profitability. Adopting a new technology that makes products faster is a change aimed at improving overall performance. Businesses do not change processes in order to increase spending, add debt, or cut wages for their own sake. Example: a manufacturer that installs a system producing finished goods three times faster than before changed its process to improve performance.

A SWOT analysis examines a business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats, so it covers both internal factors (strengths and weaknesses) and external factors (opportunities and threats). A PESTEL analysis looks only at external factors: political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal. A balance sheet or financial report shows financial condition, not the full industry picture. Example: a farm that wants to see how it stands both inside and outside the business should use a SWOT analysis rather than a PESTEL analysis.

Supply chain management is the oversight of the complete process of getting products into the marketplace, covering the flow of goods from the manufacturer all the way to the end user, including delivery. Its main steps are planning, sourcing (obtaining materials), producing, and distributing (delivering) the product. Delivery is one part of the supply chain, not the whole process. Its two main goals are maximizing the value delivered to the customer and gaining a competitive advantage by moving goods effectively and efficiently; setting prices and shaping customer perceptions are not its goals. It differs from inventory control (tracking stock on hand), production (making the goods), quality management (building quality into every activity), and risk management (preventing losses). Example: when customers complain about late deliveries, supply chain management is the area to fix, and a retailer that gets products to shelves faster and cheaper than rivals gains a competitive edge.

term: Supply Chain Manager Priority: Controlling Costs
definition: Controlling costs is the top priority of most supply chain managers and is often called the driving force of supply chain management, because it is the area where they have the most control. Keeping costs down also creates value, supports profit, and keeps the organization stable. Developing overseas markets, building a corporate image, and gaining negotiating leverage are not direct goals of supply chain management. Example: a supply chain manager renegotiates shipping contracts and consolidates suppliers to lower the cost of getting products to stores.

Centralized buying means all purchasing for a retail chain is done at one location by a central buying staff, which works well when buyers share responsibility for different product lines. It becomes ineffective when a chain grows so large that its stores are located very far apart, because one central office cannot understand the needs of every region. The fix is decentralized buying, where the country is divided into districts and district managers buy for the stores in their district. Example: a chain with stores from Maine to California lets regional buyers choose merchandise suited to local climates and tastes.

A concession is something one party gives up during a negotiation. Buyers and vendors often accept less than they wanted on one point and use that concession as leverage to get something else they want later in the talks. A concession is different from a position (what a party believes about an issue), a plea (a request), or withdrawal (passively backing away from the conflict). Example: a buyer accepts a 6 percent discount instead of the 8 percent it wanted, planning to ask for faster delivery terms in return.

term: Holding Raw Materials Inventory to Beat Price Increases
definition: One benefit of holding raw materials inventory is getting the best price on those materials. If a company expects the price of a key material to rise steadily, it should buy in bulk now and hold the raw materials, because the savings from the lower price can outweigh the carrying costs of storing them. Avoiding carrying costs is normally wise, but not when prices are climbing. Example: a power tool maker that expects steel prices to rise buys several months of steel at today's price.

A perpetual inventory is a record of inventory that is updated continuously, every time an item is added or removed, either by hand or by computer. It lets a business know at any moment how much is on hand and when to reorder. Contrast this with a physical inventory, which is the process of actually counting every item, and with inventory shrinkage, which is inventory lost through theft, breakage, or poor recordkeeping. Example: an office worker subtracts one box of pencils on the tracking sheet each time a box is taken from the supply cabinet.

A purchase order is a formal written request from a buyer to a supplier for a product or service. It spells out the quantity ordered, the price, delivery details, and contact information for both parties, so both sides have the same record and misunderstandings about what was ordered are prevented. An invoice is different: the seller sends it to request payment for goods already delivered. Example: an office that submits a purchase order for 100 reams of paper has proof of the quantity if only 80 arrive.

A retail buyer purchases merchandise for resale, and merchandise selection takes up most of the buyer's time. Selection includes identifying goods with the best resale potential, deciding what to buy and in what quantities, choosing vendors, and deciding when to buy. Buyers may also help with pricing, promotion, and managing salespeople, but those are secondary to selecting merchandise.

When a project needs tangible resources (physical items such as supplies or equipment), follow a sequence: first determine the specifications of what is needed, then check what resources you already have on hand, and only then decide whether to buy, borrow, or find an alternative and estimate the cost. Checking existing resources before buying avoids wasted money. Example: after deciding a raffle needs a roll of 200 tickets, the organizer first looks to see whether the organization already has tickets in storage.

Quality can be judged from several angles. Excellence means the product is useful and performs its job well. Value means the customer feels the product is worth the money paid. Conformance to specifications means the product meets predetermined standards, and customer satisfaction means the product meets customer wants and needs. Example: a blender that crushes ice smoothly every time demonstrates excellence, while a customer's feeling that it was a bargain reflects value.

term: Executive Commitment in a Quality Culture
definition: In an organization with a quality culture, executive level managers are personally committed and involved in quality and take responsibility for it themselves. They do not hand that responsibility off to lower managers or outside contractors, even though they may use help from others. Example: a CEO who reviews quality data every month and joins improvement meetings shows the leadership that a quality culture requires.

term: Quality Control Strategies (Internal, External, Concurrent, Feedback)
definition: Businesses control quality in several ways. Internal control relies on employees themselves: they help set quality guidelines and work with supervisors to solve problems and improve. External control relies on managers supervising employees and tying rewards to performance. Concurrent control monitors work while it is being done and corrects it on the spot. Feedback control evaluates work after it is finished and points out what went wrong. Example: employees who wrote their own customer service guidelines and meet with supervisors to improve them are using internal control.

term: Accident Response Priority: Attend to Injuries First
definition: When a workplace accident happens, the first priority is responding to the medical needs of the injured person. Looking up company protocol, calling human resources, and finding out how the accident occurred are all important, but they come after the injury has been attended to. Example: if a coworker falls and hurts their leg, help them and get medical aid first, then report the incident.

term: First Aid Steps: Check the Scene First
definition: When providing first aid, the very first step is to check the scene for safety so you do not become a second victim or cause more harm. Next, obtain consent, form an initial impression, and put on any personal protective equipment. Only then do you check the person for responsiveness, ask about signs and symptoms, and give care based on the condition found. Example: before helping someone who collapsed near a spill, make sure the floor and surroundings are safe.

term: Pilferage vs. Shoplifting, Burglary, and Robbery
definition: Pilferage is the theft of small sums of money or inexpensive items from a business, often by employees, such as taking office supplies home for personal use. Shoplifting is theft of goods by customers. Burglary is illegally entering a building to commit theft. Robbery is theft that uses force, violence, or fear. Example: employees who routinely take pens, paper, and snacks from the supply closet for home use are committing pilferage.

A business can reduce credit card fraud at the point of sale by verifying the cardholder's identification. The employee asks for another form of ID, such as a driver's license, and compares the signature or photo with the card to confirm the customer is the authorized cardholder. Credit limits are set by the card issuer, not the store, and reviewing receipts at closing or conducting audits happens after the sale, so they do not stop fraud at the register.

term: Preventing Identity Theft: Secure Web Browsers and Unique Passwords
definition: Identity theft happens when someone obtains and uses another person's information, such as credit card numbers, without consent. To reduce the risk, employees and consumers should use secure web browsers and secure (https) sites when entering payment information online, and use many unique passwords rather than a single password everywhere. Keeping records on paper does not prevent identity theft, because paper can be stolen too, and a bad credit history is a result of identity theft, not a defense against it.

term: Protecting Digital Assets: Inventory of Digital Information
definition: One effective way to protect a company's digital assets is to make an inventory of its digital information: a list of what sensitive data exists and where it is stored. Knowing where data lives helps a company respond to a breach and reveals security weaknesses. Other good practices include backing up data frequently (once a year is not enough) and limiting access to sensitive data to the people who need it. Letting employees use personal devices for work or giving everyone full access increases risk. Example: an IT team lists every server and cloud folder holding customer records and who can access each.

Security problems such as theft, burglary, fraud, and data breaches are a serious risk because the financial losses they cause can be so large that a business is forced to close. That is why businesses invest in preventing security problems instead of simply reacting to them. A business hit with major security losses cannot expand, and moving or reorganizing will not stop the losses unless the security problem itself is fixed. Example: a small shop that loses thousands of dollars of merchandise each month to shoplifting may not survive without better security measures.

The ultimate responsibility for personal health and safety on the job rests with the individual worker. A company can install safe equipment, provide training, and write safe operating procedures, but it cannot force each employee to act safely. The government passes safety laws but cannot monitor every worker, and a union can only encourage safe habits. Example: a warehouse provides back braces and lifting training, but it is up to each employee to actually use proper lifting technique.

Planning a project before starting it has several positive impacts. It increases transparency, because a written plan lets everyone see the project's scope and deliverables and encourages people to share knowledge and speak up when roadblocks appear. It also keeps the team organized, improves communication, keeps stakeholders engaged, and helps the team avoid the problems that come from cutting corners. Example: a project plan shared with the whole team makes it clear who is responsible for each task and when it is due.

The business environment, meaning the world outside the project such as the market, customers, seasons, and competitors, can change how a project is planned. Planners must consider these outside conditions when setting schedules and priorities. Example: an apartment company schedules a new building to open right before the college year begins so students can lease it, which shows the market environment shaping the project timeline.

A complete project evaluation looks at more than customer satisfaction and scope; it also checks finances by comparing the project's budget with actual income and expenses. Evaluating the budget is the only way to know whether a project was a financial success. Asking participants what they enjoyed or reviewing the schedule tells you about other aspects of the project but not about money. Example: after a school dance, the organizer compares ticket revenue with what was spent on the venue, music, and decorations to see whether it made money.

Sometimes a project cannot obtain all the financial support that was planned. The most realistic response is to look for ways to cut costs so the project can still go forward: substitute less expensive materials for costly ones, do without some supplies, or scale back extras. Lowering expectations, shortening the timeline, or eliminating the project are usually unnecessary because substitutions can still deliver the result. Example: an event team that gets half its budget rents simpler decorations instead of canceling the event.

Some CRM programs let customers voluntarily enter and update their own information, such as preferences, interests, and comments. The main benefit to the business is that customers use this opening to offer suggestions and new ideas, including requests for new services. The customer also feels in control of their own information, which builds trust. Example: a bank's online profile page invites customers to note what services they wish the bank offered, giving the bank fresh ideas for new products.

A brand promise is the specific benefit customers can expect from using a product and dealing with the company. Successful brands use the brand promise to connect with customers on an emotional, gut level rather than a purely logical or rational one. Customers stay loyal to brands they feel share their values and beliefs. Example: an outdoor gear company promises adventure and freedom, so customers feel a personal bond with the brand rather than just comparing prices.

A brand touchpoint is any point of contact between a business and a customer or potential customer. Advertisements, publicity, word of mouth, conversations with salespeople, the company website, and the product itself are all touchpoints. Things that customers never actually encounter, such as the company's internal culture, are not touchpoints, and a competitor's coupon is a touchpoint for the competitor, not for you. Example: an online ad for a candy company's chocolate is a touchpoint because the customer sees and interacts with it.

term: Positive Customer Relations Requires Being Proactive
definition: Positive customer relations require a business to be proactive: it must anticipate questions, complaints, and problems and stay ahead of them rather than simply reacting after they happen. A satisfied customer is not automatically a loyal one, since one good purchase does not guarantee repeat business; loyalty comes from consistently exceeding expectations. Customers return for reasons beyond price, such as service level and product quality, and customer relations involve every touchpoint (website, invoices, promotions), not just selling. Example: a company that emails setup tips before a new customer has a chance to get confused is being proactive.

To provide the right type and level of service, a finance professional should first ask: what are the client's expectations? Knowing the level of service and communication a client wants makes it possible to meet those needs and build a long term relationship. Ongoing communication, including following up to answer questions and resolve problems, supports this. Questions about the professional's own career goals or personal returns do not help serve the client.

term: Difficult Customer Types: Suspicious, Domineering, Slow, Disagreeable
definition: Employees meet several types of difficult customers. Suspicious customers question everything an employee tells them and want facts and proof before they believe it; they are hard to help but can become very loyal once convinced. Domineering or superior customers are overly self confident. Slow or methodical customers need a lot of time to decide because of shyness or difficulty making choices. Disagreeable customers are unpleasant, argumentative, impatient, or insulting. Example: a shopper who demands to see the written warranty before believing a product is covered is a suspicious customer.

term: Offer an Alternative Solution to Complaints
definition: When a customer's exact request cannot be met, focus on what you can do for the customer rather than what you cannot. Offer an alternative solution, such as a complimentary amenity while the problem is fixed, instead of explaining at length why the request is impossible, inspecting to see whether the complaint is valid, or blaming other staff. Those responses do not help the customer and can make the situation worse. Example: a fully booked hotel cannot move a guest to a new room, so the clerk offers free breakfast while housekeeping recleans the room.

Employees should follow a set order when handling a complaint: (1) listen attentively to the customer, (2) thank the customer for bringing the problem to your attention, which helps calm an angry customer, (3) restate the complaint in your own words to show understanding, (4) promptly investigate the problem and check company policy, (5) explain the policy to the customer, and (6) explain the plan of action and take that action. Example: after hearing a fan's complaint about slow service, a stadium employee first thanks the fan for speaking up, then repeats the problem back to confirm it.

term: Accommodating Special Requests Generates Word of Mouth
definition: When a business honors a customer's special request, it creates an exceptional experience, and the likely result is that the customer generates positive word of mouth by telling other potential customers. It is unlikely that other customers will feel treated unfairly, that the customer will become more demanding, or that the company will look inadequate. Example: a hotel that arranges a gluten free birthday cake for a guest often gains a glowing online review.

The attitude employees project toward customers is a major factor in the relationship a business builds with its customers. Friendly, polite, and helpful employees create positive customer relations, while employees who seem bored or ignore customers damage those relations. Factors like where suppliers are located or what competitors do are not what shape a business's own customer relationships. Example: a store greeter who smiles and offers help leaves shoppers with a positive impression of the whole store.

term: Reinforce Company Image by Living Company Values
definition: Employees reinforce a company's image when their actions match the values the company promotes. If a company stands for honesty and exceptional service, an employee who openly admits a mistake and then goes above and beyond to fix it is strengthening the image, not damaging it. Hiding a mistake or refusing to correct it because someone else caused it would contradict those values. Example: a hotel clerk who admits a lost reservation and upgrades the guest at no charge reinforces a reputation for honesty and service.

term: Orientation Purpose: General Information and Motivation
definition: A group orientation session for new employees gives an overview of the business, makes new hires feel welcome, and helps motivate them to do their best. It usually includes a handbook that repeats the information presented. Orientation is meant to provide general information only: it is not the place for in depth training, explaining each specific job's duties, or collecting employee input about company processes. Example: on the first day, all new hires attend a session on company history, values, and policies, then later receive job specific training from their supervisors.

Several ongoing business trends shape the work of human resources management: globalization (companies hiring and operating across countries), constantly developing new technology, company restructuring to save money, and rising costs of doing business. HR must respond to each of these, for example by recruiting internationally or retraining workers for new systems. Example: a growing trend toward globalization means an HR department must handle hiring, pay, and legal rules for employees in several countries.

When a manager resolves an employee complaint, the manager should document it so there is proof of how the problem was handled. The record should cover all the critical aspects of the complaint and how it was resolved, and a copy belongs in the employee's personnel file or a master complaint file. The documentation does not need to be lengthy, it should be kept rather than discarded, and it is the manager's responsibility rather than something to delegate. Example: a brief written summary of a scheduling complaint and its resolution can be very useful if a grievance or lawsuit arises later.

Recruitment is seeking out and attracting potential employees, for example by posting job openings on the company website or on employment websites such as Indeed. Selection is the next step: identifying the most qualified candidates through screening and interviewing. Training teaches employees how to do their jobs, and performance management evaluates how well they do them. Example: posting an advertisement for an open position on an employment website is using technology for recruitment, not selection.

During screening, employers review applications and resumes to pick the best candidates, then contact the references the applicant listed. The purpose of contacting references, such as former employers, is to verify that the information the applicant provided is accurate, for example that they really did the work they claimed. Reference checks are not used to collect personal data, determine training needs, or compare job descriptions. Example: a manager calls an applicant's previous supervisor to confirm the applicant's job title and dates of employment.

term: Benefits of Maintaining a Code of Ethics
definition: Maintaining a code of ethics produces measurable benefits for an organization: improved employee loyalty (people like belonging to ethical companies and avoid unethical ones), higher organizational integrity, greater legal compliance, and better office morale. Ethical workplaces also have an easier time attracting and keeping good employees. Example: a company that consistently follows its ethics code sees lower turnover because employees trust how they will be treated.

Supervising staff means overseeing and directing the daily activities of employees so that the work of the business gets done effectively and on time. It is the main way managers make sure the business's goals are actually accomplished. Managers delegate authority to others so they have time to supervise, and they share knowledge with employees to help them do the work. Example: a store manager who checks on each department during a shift and redirects employees to unfinished tasks is supervising staff.

Agents are intermediaries that producers hire to perform channel functions such as selling, storing, and grading, without ever taking title to (owning) the goods they handle. Using an agent lets the producer focus on production while the agent handles distribution tasks. Agents may sell to retailers, wholesalers, or distributors, but it is the producer who hires them. Example: a small fruit grower hires a produce agent to sell its crop to grocery chains.

Marketing information is all the marketing related data available from inside and outside a business, covering both past situations and what is happening now. One major advantage of using it is that managers can predict risks that may occur in the future and take steps to control them. Preparing reports is something managers do with the information, not a benefit of having it, and marketing information is not used to train employees or understand regulations. Example: data showing a product is losing popularity lets a business repackage it before customers leave.

A competitive analysis examines competitors' activities to identify their strengths and weaknesses and, from that, the company's own opportunities and threats in the marketplace. It is the tool to use when a company wants to know whether rivals selling similar products are taking its market share. If the analysis shows lost share, the company then looks at its own weaknesses and takes corrective action. Internal financial data and the existing marketing plan do not provide current information about competitors. Example: a shoe store that tracks a new competitor's prices, promotions, and customer traffic is conducting a competitive analysis.

Businesses often set prices based on the customers they want to attract. Discount pricing appeals to shoppers focused on low prices, while regular or premium pricing appeals to shoppers who expect a higher quality experience. Profit decisions focus on profitability and return on investment, promotional decisions involve stimulating demand, and place decisions involve shipping, handling, and where products are available. Example: Walmart's low prices and Target's higher prices each reflect a decision about which customers to attract.

One effective, low cost way to learn more about a company's target market is to brainstorm with your own staff. Employees are customers too, and they can offer insight into the wants, needs, and values of the people the business serves. Talking only to young people helps only if young people are your target market, and advertising or hiring an accounting firm does not reveal anything about customers. Example: a cafe owner holds a staff session to gather ideas about what regular customers want from a new menu.

A market is all the individuals or organizations that have needs to satisfy and the willingness and ability to spend money to satisfy them. A consumer market is made up of individuals buying for personal use, while an industrial market is made up of businesses. This is different from an economic system (how a country makes economic decisions), a cooperative (a business owned by its customers), or a corporate chain (similar stores owned by one corporation). Example: everyone willing to pay for a smartphone makes up the smartphone market.

The marketing mix is the combination of product, price, place, and promotion decisions a business uses to reach its target market. When the environment changes, a business reviews each element: product questions ask how trends will affect what it sells, price questions ask whether list prices should change, promotion questions ask about the advertising budget and message, and place questions ask how products reach customers, including the costs and benefits of the channel of distribution. Example: asking whether to sell through retailers or directly online is a place decision.

Marketing is often described as creating exchanges: it encourages trade by giving buyers and sellers opportunities to swap something of value, usually a product for money. Marketing does not create needs; it identifies and satisfies needs that already exist. It uses advertisements as one tool, and it bridges the gap between producers and customers. Example: a farmers market lets growers and shoppers exchange fresh produce for cash, which is marketing at its most basic.

Marketing-information management is the marketing function responsible for gathering, accessing, synthesizing, evaluating, and disseminating data for use in making business decisions. It makes sure products are actually meeting the needs and wants of customers. It is different from product/service management (developing and improving the product mix) and from management in general (planning, organizing, directing, and controlling resources). Example: a company surveys customers, analyzes the results, and shares the findings with the product team.

A price must work for both sides of an exchange. If it is too high, customers feel cheated and walk away; if it is too low, the seller cannot cover costs or earn a profit. When a business strikes the right pricing balance, the exchange is beneficial to both the customer and the seller: the customer gets fair value and the seller earns a reasonable return. Example: a coffee shop that prices a latte so that customers see it as worth the money and the shop still earns a healthy margin has found the right balance.

The product mix is all the different goods and services a company makes or sells. A product line is a group of closely related products within that mix, and a product item is one specific model or brand. When a business changes the type and amount of services it offers, it is changing its product mix. The promotional mix, by contrast, is the combination of promotion types a business uses. Example: a bank that adds investment advising to its checking, savings, and loan services has expanded its product mix.

Products sold to individuals who will use them personally are sold for ultimate consumption. This differs from products sold for resale (bought by intermediaries to sell to their own customers), for industrial purposes (bought by businesses to make other products or run operations), or for promotional purposes (display or advertising items). Example: a family buying a refrigerator for their kitchen is buying for ultimate consumption, while a restaurant buying the same model for its kitchen is an industrial purchase.

The public relations function builds goodwill between a business and its various publics. One way to build goodwill with the community is to support charitable events by donating money, goods, or volunteers. This is a public relations activity, not selling, advertising, or a media blitz (an intense effort to spread a message through every channel). Example: a snack company that donates energy bars to runners in a charity race is doing public relations for a charitable cause.

Promotion serves three main purposes: to inform customers about a company or product, to persuade them to buy, and to remind them that the company and its products exist. Reminding matters for established products that customers might otherwise forget. Promotion may sometimes reassure customers about a problem, but it is never used to warn or caution customers away from a product. Example: a long running soft drink brand keeps advertising mainly to remind shoppers it is still there.

A rebate is a sales promotion that returns part of the price a customer paid after the sale, usually offered by the manufacturer. It differs from a coupon (a certificate that discounts the price at the time of purchase), a markdown (a reduction in the selling price at the point of sale), and a sweepstakes (a game of chance with a prize). Example: a bakery that offers $2.00 back after a customer buys a slow selling pie is using a rebate.

A marketing objective is a specific, measurable goal. Businesses set several types: sales objectives (increase units sold), profit objectives (raise margins), promotion objectives (boost awareness), distribution objectives (add outlets), and product objectives (improve the product or service itself). A goal to improve service by a set percentage is a product oriented objective because service is part of what the company offers. Example: a hotel chain aiming to raise its guest satisfaction score by 15 percent has set a product oriented marketing objective.

The directing function of management benefits an organization mainly by coordinating employees' work and effort. Without direction, employees tend to work in isolation, which leads to duplicated tasks and lower efficiency. Other benefits belong to other functions: planning sets company goals, organizing makes sure everyone knows their role, and controlling lets managers check progress. Example: a shift supervisor assigns each worker a station and keeps the crew working toward the same daily target.

The change management approach is a structured way of planning, implementing, and supporting change so that it is carried out in the best possible way and produces long term benefits. It covers communicating the need for change, preparing employees, and following through after the change is made. It is not the same as general problem solving or solution finding, and it is the opposite of change avoidance. Example: a company adopting new software uses a change management approach with training, feedback sessions, and a phased rollout.

Effective business plans share four characteristics. They are flexible, so they can be adjusted quickly when conditions change. They are simple enough that every team member can understand them. They are feasible, meaning realistic given available resources. And they are goal aligned, supporting the organization's ultimate objectives. Example: a nonprofit that loses expected grant money and quickly redirects its building plan is relying on the flexibility of its plan.

Businesses use four types of resources. Natural resources are found in nature (land, water, minerals). Human resources are the people who work to produce goods or services. Financial resources are all the sources of money available to the business. Material resources are the equipment and supplies used in operations, including computers and software systems. Example: a digital record keeping system set up by an HR manager is a material resource, even though it is used to manage people.

Organizational change management is planned, organization wide change to a major part of the company to increase individual and organizational effectiveness. When change is implemented well, it raises worker morale and motivation, encourages teamwork, and enriches jobs. Higher morale improves the quality of work, which shortens production cycles and lowers costs. Organizational change affects all employees, not just some, and its effects are deep and long lasting rather than brief. Example: a company that carefully rolls out a new teamwork structure sees employees more engaged a year later.

Knowledge is an intangible combination of human experiences, insights, and intuitions that gives a person a framework for interpreting and reacting to the world. It is the result of long term learning that has been retained and applied to real situations. Training teaches a specific skill, innovation creates something new, and recruiting attracts job candidates, but expertise built over years of experience is a form of knowledge. Example: a veteran employee whose deep understanding of operations lets him improve results is applying knowledge.

Businesses usually have three levels of managers. Executive (top level) managers are responsible for the whole organization and spend most of their time setting goals and doing strategic planning. Mid level managers implement the goals set by executives and link the top and bottom levels; regional managers are usually mid level. First line (supervisory) managers work directly with the employees who do the routine work and spend most of their time staffing, directing, and controlling day to day activities. Example: a shift supervisor at a restaurant is a first line manager.

A conflict of interest arises when a manager's personal relationships or interests make it hard to be objective in a business decision. Making a decision about an employee who is a friend is a classic example, because the manager may not want to give a deserved negative evaluation. The ethical response is for the manager to step aside and let a manager who is not the employee's friend handle the decision. Example: a supervisor asks a colleague to conduct the performance review of a close friend on her team.

Acting ethically while starting a business brings concrete advantages: a lower risk of harming the environment, greater support and loyalty from customers, and a lower risk of lawsuits. Ethical decision making also protects the entrepreneur's reputation and makes it easier to attract employees and investors. These benefits come from ethical choices, not from the type of legal structure chosen or the experience level of the people hired. Example: a startup that properly disposes of chemical waste avoids fines and earns the trust of the community.

Before hiring a first employee, a business owner should figure out what work needs to be done (bookkeeping, purchasing, ad placement, and so on) and how often each task is performed. From that, the owner can decide whether the workload calls for a full time employee or whether a part time employee could handle it. Only after settling the type and amount of work can the owner recruit applicants and evaluate their education or trustworthiness. Example: a growing business owner asks whether there is enough work for a full time assistant before posting the job.

Entrepreneurs who build their businesses on strong ethical principles are far less likely to face legal problems later. Trying to cheat the system when starting a business, such as hiding income, skipping required licenses, or misleading investors, may seem like a shortcut, but it usually leads to legal trouble, not big profits, customer loyalty, or protection from the law. Example: a founder who falsifies records to avoid taxes risks fines, lawsuits, and even losing the business.

Ethical behavior is crucial for entrepreneurs because customers expect the companies they support to act ethically toward their communities, the environment, and the world. Winning customer trust is hard for a new company, so an ethical workplace culture helps an entrepreneur stand out from competitors. Many investors also support only companies that show a commitment to ethics. Unethical behavior may pay off briefly, but it is unsustainable and damages the business over time.

term: Going Public (IPO) as an Exit Strategy
definition: An initial public offering (IPO) is when a business owner sells stock to the public, giving up some or all control as the venture becomes a public corporation. A public corporation must follow strict government rules, including forming a board of directors to guide the company. An entrepreneur who wants to step back from daily operations but stay involved can serve on the board of directors, which also makes the transition smoother. The board, not the founder alone, appoints the president or successor. Example: a founder who takes her company public and then joins its board keeps a voice in major decisions without running day to day activities.

term: Licensing Fee as a Percentage of Startup Costs
definition: The time, money, and fees needed to start a business vary with the type of business. When a licensee must pay a licensor an initial fee, the entrepreneur can measure how large that fee is compared with all startup costs by dividing the fee by total startup costs. Example: an initial licensing fee of $11,250 on total startup costs of $75,000 is $11,250 divided by $75,000, which equals 0.15, or 15 percent of startup costs.

Nepotism is using your power or influence to benefit friends or relatives, such as hiring people you know personally instead of the most qualified applicants. It is a form of unfairness and subjectivity, the opposite of objective hiring. Small business owners are especially at risk because they often know their applicants. Example: a new owner hires her cousin and two friends for open positions without interviewing outside candidates; that is nepotism, not fairness or objectivity.

term: Startup Employees Make or Break Success
definition: In a new business venture, employees have a very large impact on success because a small team does almost everything. Entrepreneurs who treat employees ethically and keep them happy and engaged in the company's mission are more likely to attract and retain quality workers. Overworking employees to squeeze out profit is unethical, and happy employees are not necessarily customers of the business. Example: a five person startup losing its best developer can stall the entire product launch.

term: Management Experience and Span of Control
definition: The number of direct reports a manager can handle depends partly on how much management experience the manager has. Experienced managers have developed the skills to guide, monitor, and support many employees at once, so they can take on a wider span of control. A new manager often struggles with even a few direct reports simply because of inexperience, not because of a lack of ability. Example: a first year manager overseeing one employee may feel stretched while a ten year veteran comfortably oversees six.
